SA Express - We Do Nothing For You

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SA Express is pending liquidation. Most employees have not been paid since February. They too are now penniless and who knows, soon to be homeless. A plea to government is falling on deaf ears.

Unique Selling Point:
With the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) keeping their distance and the acting CEO deferring to the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP), workers have been left holding the can. Business Rescue has revealed the shocking shortcuts taken in the past... UIF not paid, employees' medical aid not uptodate. The COVID19 pandemic was not the cause of this but in the current crisis the SA Express employees have the worst of all head-starts on the rest of South Africa - out of work, money running out, bills unpaid, food running out and no support from the state, banks or erstwhile employers. From the employees' perspective, nobody cares, not the DPE nor the BRPs. There is no money, so can the government come to the rescue of these loyal employees?

Summary:
After being put into business rescue most SA Express employees have been left without salaries since the end of February where some were paid 50% of their salaries, but as of the 25th of March 462 of the 650 employees have received no salary at all. They were told this on the 24th of March through a letter from the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP). It was a very matter-of-fact letter informing them to speak to the banks that they will not be able to meet their commitments. They were unable to claim from UIF or get benefits from their pensions and medical aids, as those had not been paid. Many of these employees support families and are on chronic medication, they are running out of food and do not know where to turn to. They have written letters to the DPE and to the President and as yet they have had no response. The BRP Daniel Terblanche and Phahlani Mkhombo say their hands are tied as there is no money despite appeals to the shareholder which is government for some cash injection. They have applied for COVID relief for UIF, but that won't even cover some of these employees' actual UIF claims and they are still waiting to hear if there will be any relief from the COVID fund. This afternoon the BRP's managed to get an extension on two of the medical aid schemes until May, but there are still others that have not been covered. SA Express employees have basically been left out in the cold.

Pappa Mollo who is acting on behalf of the employees is willing to speak to Carte Blanche

And they are trying to see if they can bring charges of fraud against the government with
Regards to the fact that their UIF contributions had been deducted from the salaries they
Received, as well as pensions and Medical Aid. Is government going to let these loyal
Employees fend for themselves?

Further information:
I have requested interviews with the BRP, as the acting CEO for SA Express Thuli Mpshe says she is not mandated to speak. The BRP Daniel Terblanche says that he has to ask legal advice as to whether he can speak to us, but I will send him questions in writing.
I have requested an interview with the DPE and Minister Pravin Gordhan. I have been told that there is a Cabinet meeting on Monday and that SA Express may be addressed, but the BRP says that SA Express is not on the agenda. We will only know after Monday, I have requested the interview with the Minister for Tuesday, which may or may not improve the situation of the employees.
Case Studies
Pappa Mollo is an engineer and is basically without income and support for his family, he is speaking on behalf of employees as many are afraid to show their faces and has been the liaison on their behalf.
Moerida, has worked for SA Express for 26 years and is an Internal Quality Auditor, she says she gave her life to the company, even when they ran out of money, she paid out of her own credit card so that pilots could complete their training, that is the level of loyalty and dedication she gave to the company. She is a single mother, and also supports her father and an adopted child. She is on chronic diabetic medication and has been unable to get medicine. The only way her family is getting food is from her brother-in-law, basically she has nothing left.
Sello Seala is based in Bloemfontein at the Braam Fischer Airport and is a customer service agent, he has worked for the company for 10 years. He supports his family and two children. Currently they have no money and he can't even buy salt. I can do a skype interview with him, and he said he can shoot some cell phone footage of his life and his family.
Asaf is also an employee who is getting me another case study as well.

Press Release:


With no salaries paid in March and no money for their rent, food and chronic medication – hundreds of SA Express employees are in despair as the airline faces liquidation.

Script:


Sello: I'm living on handouts [the fridge] it's embarrassing when one does not have salt in the house. Even when I'm talking to you right now I'm getting emotional. I have two sons, they left because there was no food in the house. They are now staying with their maternal grandmother. So it's bad, it's bad.

VO: Hearing Sello Seala's story you would think this is another COVID-19 tragedy. But Sello has been a loyal employee of State-owned airline SA Express for 11 years. Like most of the around 700 employees, he has not received a salary since the end of February.

Sello: Not only is my immediate family affected, even my extended family is affected.

Link: In February this year for the first time ever, a state owned enterprise, SA Express, was placed in business rescue by one of its creditors, Ziegler SA which is owed R11.3 million by the airline. Now after failing to get government money for a bailout, the business rescue practitioners had no option but to apply for the airline's liquidation on the 25th of March.
Actual Letter from BRP
Delay in payment of March 2020 staff salaries
The adverse operational challenges that SA Express faced in the last month, exacerbated by the impact of the spread of corona virus on passenger demand, have affected the airline’s ability to generate adequate cash to fund critical operational expenses as they became due. The challenge to generate cash was further amplified by the suspension of operations on the 19th March 2020.

VO: On the eve of that application, SA Express employees received communication from the Business Rescue Practitioners, Daniel Terblanche and Phahlani Mkombo, citing that due to operational challenges, exacerbated by the impact of the spread of coronavirus, that their salaries, due on the 25th of March, would be delayed.
Employee Representative and Maintenance Engineer at SA Express Papa Mollo was dismayed by the news.

Pappa: You can imagine, I mean the 24th, most of us are already anxious about our pay.

VO: The notice went on to say that they were waiting for a response on a request for emergency funding from the Department of Public Enterprises, and that SA Express was obliged to pay wages within seven days
Pappa: We were never told that we're not going to get paid. So we anticipated that it would be within the seven days that was indicated on the letter.

VO: But seven days went by and still no salaries were received.
In a written response to Carte Blanche regarding the plight of the staff, the BRP's state that "There is no plan in place to support the families under the current circumstances, the shareholder is not willing to advance any funds to the Company to relieve the plight of the employees."

Masa: The BRPs and the acting CEO say they did communicate to the employees that they actually may not get paid.

Pappa: Yes, the possibilities might have been there. But When you saying my salary has been delayed, you are giving me hope that you gonna be paying me?

VO: The BRPs emphasised that from the start they have been open with employees about the risk of salaries not being paid. They were committed to paying salaries, but after numerous failed attempts to secure post-commencement finance from the shareholder, it was impossible to do so.

Dr V : South African Express used to be a very profitable airline. But from 2012 onwards, it's mandate was changed from a pure commercial mandate to include the so called development mandate.

VO: Independent aviation economist Dr Joachim Vermooten has followed the airline’s journey since its inception in 1994.

Dr V: Government wanted to increase its role in the economy So a total upscaling of the operation.

VO: SA Express’s ambition for growth increased their capacity, but in South Africa there was not enough demand. In due course, amidst growing operational challenges and lack of funds, the airline was also steeped in corruption and mismanagement.

Dr V: it was claimed that a 2.4 billion fuel contract was awarded to I think a music producer. It's also very documented that South African Express was used as a conduit for siphoning off monies paid from North West to South African Express.

VO: In 2018 SA Express received around a 1.2 billion rand state bailout, but were instructed to use the funds to pay off government guaranteed debt, leaving the airline with no operational capital.

Dr V: At the end of the day its operational safety aspects were very concerning and the Civil Aviation Authority moved in and grounded the airline.

VO: The airline received a further 300 million rands in September 2019, by which time their debt had become unmanageable.

Michael: So the people who are actually suffering in this situation are not the people who are responsible for the situation

VO: IT Business Analyst Michael Hlatswayo has been with SA Express since 1997 and is part of the team representing thee unpaid staff.

Masa: Do you feel the employees are the ones who are left to bear the brunt now?

Michael: Sadly, yes, sadly yes. As you can see, I'm at my in-laws right now because I cannot afford rent anywhere.

Link: Four weeks have passed and most SA Express employees have still not been paid. Many of them are living hand to mouth, especially now during lockdown.

VO: Moerieda Davids has worked for thee airline for 26 yeers and is now an Internal auditor for the Quality
Assurance Department.
Moerida: I used to be a crew planner, and our pilots go overseas to do their training.. So we used to personally use our credit cards, just to make sure the pilots get there and have accommodation so that they can get the training because if they don't get the training, they get grounded, and then the aircraft gets grounded. Everybody did their little bit to make sure SA Express stayed in the air.

VO: A single mother, Moerieda has adopted a 2 year old boy, and looks after another child whose family has no means. She also takes care of her father.

Moerida: The day before lockdown, I had R250 to my name. That was it. So not only are we not having cash, but we now have to pay for the debit orders that have already gone off.

Sello: Yesterday was Sunday. I woke up, tears were just falling down my face. It was just coming down. We have a group chat as colleagues and then I told them guys I feel so messed up, the tears are just coming down.


Michael: We have a situation where people have got little children, and they cannot afford to buy baby formula or food.

VO:Michael and Papa, together with thee employees on the chat group, embarked on a crowdfunding campaign to assist colleagues most in need.

Pappa: What we are doing is we are getting 500 rand vouchers per person. As we all know, that doesn't even fill a basket. But with our given situations, I truly believe that it went a long way.

VO: Employees say they are unable to claim from UIF, and their pensions and medical aids were frozen, as SA Express failed to make those payments, even though they were deducted from their payslips.

Pappa: Why is the UIF money deducted from the employees and not paid to the UIF?

VO: The Business Rescue practitioners confirmed
that this was in fact the case, and that "the Company historically failed to make any UIF contributions for an extended period - this was the position prior to business rescue proceedings."

However, the BRP's managed to extend the cover for two of the medical aids to month end. Moerieda and her father are both diabetics and her father depends on her for financial support.

Moerida: he's on medication, none of which he's got this month because I didn't have the money
Masa: How's your dad going to survive without the meds?

Moerida: He's not because his sugar levels we've taken and yesterday it was on 27. And he can go to a sugar diabetic coma anytime.

Link: At the eleventh hour, the Department of Public Enterprises seems to have come up with a plan for staff salaries.

VO: They sent a response in writing on Thursday the 23rd of April, stating that there is some payout forthcoming from the UIF, adding "regrettably this situation is the result of wholesale corruption at this entity for which the people concerned still have to face consequences."

Actual letter for reference only
"The Department is working with the The BRPs and leadership teams at the airline to ensure that the business is able to meet its obligations

The airline has applied for UIF support, and the Department is supporting the application. There has been some payout by UIF.

DPE is trying everything in its ability to ensure the welfare of employees.

We will continue to persuade the UIF to support these efforts to ensure the workers have adequate income.

Regrettably this situation is the result of wholesale corruption at this entity for which the people concerned still have to face consequences."

VO: On hearing of the UIF payment of 5.7 million Rands, unions NUMSA and SACCA were outraged as the monthly SA Express salary bill amounts to around R25 Million.

Zazi: it seems that every SAX employee will get a maximum of around R7000 each which of course is unable to cover their basic needs. Someone needs to come to the party you know including the shareholder.

Phakamile: For months and years in advance we raised the alarm about decision making, about poor management, about looting, about corruption and we were ignored. And it’s now members and ordinary families who must pay the highest price because of a failure in leadership.

Zazi: We believe we've worked very hard in order to develop some sort of viable plan in order to save SAX and it would just be from a lack of willingness should SAX not be saved.


Masa: would it be best to liquidate it or just try and save it?

Dr V: I think there's not much to save it to be honest. By the time that the business rescue practitioners got involved it was already too late. Had they been brought in two or three years ago, it might have been a totally different matter.

VO: But liquidation is the last thing that the distressed SA Express employees want to face.

Sello: It's gonna be hard because people that are most affected that is my family. My life will be destroyed.

So we used to personally use our credit cards, just to make sure the pilots get there and have accommodation so that they can get the training because if they don't get the training, they get grounded, and then the aircraft gets grounded. Everybody did their little bit to make sure SA Express stayed in the air. VO: A single mother, Moerieda has adopted a 2 year old boy, and looks after another child whose family has no means. She also takes care of her father. Moerida: The day before lockdown, I had R250 to my name. That was it. So not only are we not having cash, but we now have to pay for the debit orders that have already gone off. Sello: Yesterday was Sunday. I woke up, tears were just falling down my face. It was just coming down. We have a group chat as colleagues and then I told them guys I feel so messed up, the tears are just coming down. Michael: We have a situation where people have got little children, and they cannot afford to buy baby formula or food. VO:Michael and Papa, together with thee employees on the chat group, embarked on a crowdfunding campaign to assist colleagues most in need. Pappa: What we are doing is we are getting 500 rand vouchers per person. As we all know, that doesn't even fill a basket. But with our given situations, I truly believe that it went a long way. VO: Employees say they are unable to claim from UIF, and their pensions and medical aids were frozen, as SA Express failed to make those payments, even though they were deducted from their payslips. Pappa: Why is the UIF money deducted from the employees and not paid to the UIF? VO: The Business Rescue practitioners confirmed that this was in fact the case, and that "the Company historically failed to make any UIF contributions for an extended period - this was the position prior to business rescue proceedings." However, the BRP's managed to extend the cover for two of the medical aids to month end. Moerieda and her father are both diabetics and her father depends on her for financial support. Moerida: he's on medication, none of which he's got this month because I didn't have the money Masa: How's your dad going to survive without the meds? Moerida: He's not because his sugar levels we've taken and yesterday it was on 27. And he can go to a sugar diabetic coma anytime. Link: At the eleventh hour, the Department of Public Enterprises seems to have come up with a plan for staff salaries. VO: They sent a response in writing on Thursday the 23rd of April, stating that there is some payout forthcoming from the UIF, adding "regrettably this situation is the result of wholesale corruption at this entity for which the people concerned still have to face consequences." Actual letter for reference only "The Department is working with the The BRPs and leadership teams at the airline to ensure that the business is able to meet its obligations The airline has applied for UIF support, and the Department is supporting the application. There has been some payout by UIF. DPE is trying everything in its ability to ensure the welfare of employees. We will continue to persuade the UIF to support these efforts to ensure the workers have adequate income. Regrettably this situation is the result of wholesale corruption at this entity for which the people concerned still have to face consequences." VO: On hearing of the UIF payment of 5.7 million Rands, unions NUMSA and SACCA were outraged as the monthly SA Express salary bill amounts to around R25 Million. Zazi: it seems that every SAX employee will get a maximum of around R7000 each which of course is unable to cover their basic needs. Someone needs to come to the party you know including the shareholder. Phakamile: For months and years in advance we raised the alarm about decision making, about poor management, about looting, about corruption and we were ignored. And it’s now members and ordinary families who must pay the highest price because of a failure in leadership. Zazi: We believe we've worked very hard in order to develop some sort of viable plan in order to save SAX and it would just be from a lack of willingness should SAX not be saved. Masa: would it be best to liquidate it or just try and save it? Dr V: I think there's not much to save it to be honest. By the time that the business rescue practitioners got involved it was already too late. Had they been brought in two or three years ago, it might have been a totally different matter. VO: But liquidation is the last thing that the distressed SA Express employees want to face. Sello: It's gonna be hard because people that are most affected that is my family. My life will be destroyed.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): SA Express is pending liquidation. Most employees have not been paid since February. They too are now penniless and who knows, soon to be homeless. A plea to government is falling on deaf ears.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: With the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) keeping their distance and the acting CEO deferring to the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP), workers have been left holding the can. Business Rescue has revealed the shocking shortcuts taken in the past... UIF not paid, employees' medical aid not uptodate. The COVID19 pandemic was not the cause of this but in the current crisis the SA Express employees have the worst of all head-starts on the rest of South Africa - out of work, money running out, bills unpaid, food running out and no support from the state, banks or erstwhile employers. From the employees' perspective, nobody cares, not the DPE nor the BRPs. There is no money, so can the government come to the rescue of these loyal employees?
metadata.Summary: After being put into business rescue most SA Express employees have been left without salaries since the end of February where some were paid 50% of their salaries, but as of the 25th of March 462 of the 650 employees have received no salary at all. They were told this on the 24th of March through a letter from the Business Rescue Practitioners (BRP). It was a very matter-of-fact letter informing them to speak to the banks that they will not be able to meet their commitments. They were unable to claim from UIF or get benefits from their pensions and medical aids, as those had not been paid. Many of these employees support families and are on chronic medication, they are running out of food and do not know where to turn to. They have written letters to the DPE and to the President and as yet they have had no response. The BRP Daniel Terblanche and Phahlani Mkhombo say their hands are tied as there is no money despite appeals to the shareholder which is government for some cash injection. They have applied for COVID relief for UIF, but that won't even cover some of these employees' actual UIF claims and they are still waiting to hear if there will be any relief from the COVID fund. This afternoon the BRP's managed to get an extension on two of the medical aid schemes until May, but there are still others that have not been covered. SA Express employees have basically been left out in the cold. Pappa Mollo who is acting on behalf of the employees is willing to speak to Carte Blanche And they are trying to see if they can bring charges of fraud against the government with Regards to the fact that their UIF contributions had been deducted from the salaries they Received, as well as pensions and Medical Aid. Is government going to let these loyal Employees fend for themselves?
metadata.Further information: I have requested interviews with the BRP, as the acting CEO for SA Express Thuli Mpshe says she is not mandated to speak. The BRP Daniel Terblanche says that he has to ask legal advice as to whether he can speak to us, but I will send him questions in writing. I have requested an interview with the DPE and Minister Pravin Gordhan. I have been told that there is a Cabinet meeting on Monday and that SA Express may be addressed, but the BRP says that SA Express is not on the agenda. We will only know after Monday, I have requested the interview with the Minister for Tuesday, which may or may not improve the situation of the employees. Case Studies Pappa Mollo is an engineer and is basically without income and support for his family, he is speaking on behalf of employees as many are afraid to show their faces and has been the liaison on their behalf. Moerida, has worked for SA Express for 26 years and is an Internal Quality Auditor, she says she gave her life to the company, even when they ran out of money, she paid out of her own credit card so that pilots could complete their training, that is the level of loyalty and dedication she gave to the company. She is a single mother, and also supports her father and an adopted child. She is on chronic diabetic medication and has been unable to get medicine. The only way her family is getting food is from her brother-in-law, basically she has nothing left. Sello Seala is based in Bloemfontein at the Braam Fischer Airport and is a customer service agent, he has worked for the company for 10 years. He supports his family and two children. Currently they have no money and he can't even buy salt. I can do a skype interview with him, and he said he can shoot some cell phone footage of his life and his family. Asaf is also an employee who is getting me another case study as well.
